title: US child SPM poverty in 2027 under current law
question: What percent of all U.S. children under 18 will be below the Supplemental Poverty Measure poverty threshold in calendar year 2027, using the methodology authenticated by the July 17, 2026 Census announcement, in the first Census annual income-and-poverty release?
resolutionSource: U.S. Census Bureau revised-SPM methodology announcement (identity) and Poverty in the United States: 2027, Supplemental Poverty Measure Table B-2 (resolving artifact)
resolutionRule: Resolve to the first Census annual income-and-poverty release artifact for CY2027 using the revised SPM methodology whose identity is authenticated by the registered 2026-07-17 Census announcement: Poverty in the United States: 2027, Supplemental Poverty Measure Table B-2, ALL RACES 2027 row, Under 18 years / Below Poverty / Percent column. The 2028-08-01 through 2028-12-31 expected release window and 2028-12-31 resolve-by deadline are Thesis lab commitments; the announcement does not establish either timing value. Record the published percent without scaling or rounding and ignore later revisions.

reasoning.text: The base rate is a persistence prior anchored on the September 2026 annual report's CY2025 child SPM rate of 13.4%. The reference class contains seven fetched calendar-year estimates under the announced corrected methodology, with the separately published population-control update for 2024. These are corrected historical estimates, not original annual vintages. Old-methodology values are excluded, and no additional hypothetical methodology adjustment is applied.

reasoning.call: Fetch https://www.irs.gov/irb/2026-38_irb and read its explanation of the child tax credit calculation.
reasoning.result: IRS describes ACTC as 15% of earned income exceeding $2,500. It states a 2025 maximum child credit of $2,200 and refundable cap of $1,700, with inflation adjustments thereafter. These amounts are not presented as fetched 2027 indexed amounts. Retaining the earnings threshold limits assistance to families with very low earnings.

CBO estimates work requirements reduce average monthly participation by 2.4 million over 2025–2034, including 300,000 adults living with children age 14 or older. Internet-expense restrictions reduce monthly benefits about $10 for 65% of households over 2026–2034. Thrifty Food Plan restrictions begin lowering benefits relative to the previous baseline in 2027. These are not isolated CY2027 child-poverty effects and are not summed mechanically.

September 2026 FOMC medians project 2027 real GDP growth of 2.4%, fourth-quarter unemployment of 4.1%, and PCE inflation of 2.3%, versus projected 2026 inflation of 3.7%. Growth and inflation are fourth-quarter-to-fourth-quarter projections, not annual averages. This supports continued growth rather than a recession central case.

reasoning.text: Prior/update/interval: Use a level-persistence prior of 13.4 from the seven-year corrected-methodology sample. Judgmental adjustments in percentage points are momentum 0.0, one-off 0.0, incremental SNAP policy effects +0.6, and macro improvement -0.1, giving 13.4 + 0.6 - 0.1 = 13.9. These adjustment magnitudes are forecasting assumptions, not official estimates; the increased child credit is already represented in the anchor. Successive historical changes are [-2.8, -4.5, 6.9, 1.5, 0.0, -0.1], with mean 0.166667 and squared deviations summing to 77.793333. Sample sigma = 3.944448 percentage points = sqrt(77.793333/5); 1.28*sigma = 5.048893. Narrow that half-width by a judgmental factor of 0.60 because emergency pandemic transfers and their reversal dominate dispersion and are not the central regime. The corrected methodology is already observed, so no speculative transition shift is added. The resulting predictive sigma of 2.366669 remains above the ordinary 2023–2025 transition sigma of 0.896289 multiplied by sqrt(2), retaining room for the two-year horizon, policy implementation, and first-print measurement risk. The nominal 80% normal interval has half-width 1.28*2.366669 = 3.029336, giving 10.870664 to 16.929336, reported as [10.87, 16.93].

Upside risk to the poverty rate comes from weaker parental employment, larger SNAP losses, or housing and medical costs outpacing earnings; a severe recession combined with benefit losses could land above 16.93%, outside the interval. Downside risk comes from stronger earnings, slower housing costs, and greater transfer uptake; unusually strong gains in family resources could land below 10.87%, outside the interval. The registered earnings-threshold condition alone does not eliminate these risks.
